claim: There were 1,792,759 laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases in the Netherlands between 22 September 2020 and 31 August 2021.
source: There were 1,792,759 laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases in the Netherlands during the study period between 22 September 2020 and 31 August 2021 (week 39/2020 to week 34/2021; Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of laboratory-confirmed cases during the study period.

claim: 39,844 SARS-CoV-2 positive nasopharyngeal samples were randomly selected and sequenced to obtain whole virus genomes as part of the national SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance program.
source: 39,844 SARS-CoV-2 positive nasopharyngeal samples were randomly selected from 25 Municipal and Regional Health Service (GGD) regions across the Netherlands during this study period and sequenced to obtain whole virus genomes as part of the national SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance program.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of samples sequenced.

claim: Most reported cases were attributed to the more densely populated regions of the country including North and South Holland, as well as North Brabant.
source: Similar to the first wave of the pandemic in the Netherlands in Spring 2020, most reported cases were attributed to the more densely populated regions of the country including North and South Holland, as well as North Brabant (Figure 1B) where the first local clusters of SARS-CoV-2 were also detected in March 2020 (Oude Munnink et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 1B showing the geographic distribution of cases.

claim: The first local clusters of SARS-CoV-2 in the Netherlands were detected in North and South Holland and North Brabant in March 2020.
source: Similar to the first wave of the pandemic in the Netherlands in Spring 2020, most reported cases were attributed to the more densely populated regions of the country including North and South Holland, as well as North Brabant (Figure 1B) where the first local clusters of SARS-CoV-2 were also detected in March 2020 (Oude Munnink et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Oude Munnink et al., 2020 to support this claim about the first local clusters.

claim: Viruses sampled at the start of the study period were largely genotyped as clade 20A and its daughter lineages, 20B and 20E (EU1).
source: Using NextClade lineage assignment (Aksamentov et al., 2021), the viruses sampled at the start of the study period were largely genotyped as clade 20 A and its daughter lineages, 20B and 20E (EU1) (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript states the genotyping results and references Figure 1B-C.

claim: 20A was the lineage that seeded the pandemic in Europe in March 2020.
source: 20 A was the lineage that seeded the pandemic in Europe in March 2020.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the 20A lineage.

claim: 20E (EU1) was first detected in Spain in June 2020 and spread widely across Europe due to the resumption of regional travel over summer 2020.
source: On the other hand, 20E (EU1) was first detected in Spain on June 2020 and spread widely across Europe due to the resumption of regional travel over summer 2020 (Hodcroft et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hodcroft et al., 2021 to support this claim about 20E (EU1).

claim: Non-pharmaceutical interventions closing restaurants and nightlife establishments were implemented on 14 October 2020.
source: Owing to rising case numbers, non-pharmaceutical interventions closing restaurants and nightlife establishments were implemented on 14 October 2020.
evidence: The manuscript states the date and nature of these interventions.

claim: The first Alpha sample was collected on 5 December 2020 in the national surveillance program.
source: The first Alpha sample was collected on 5 December 2020 in the national surveillance program prior to the full lockdown that closed all public venues, workplaces and schools on 15 December 2020.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the date of the first Alpha sample collection.

claim: A full lockdown that closed all public venues, workplaces and schools was implemented on 15 December 2020.
source: The first Alpha sample was collected on 5 December 2020 in the national surveillance program prior to the full lockdown that closed all public venues, workplaces and schools on 15 December 2020.
evidence: The manuscript states the date and nature of the full lockdown.

claim: A curfew was imposed on 23 January 2021.
source: A curfew was also imposed later on 23 January 2021.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the date of curfew implementation.

claim: A sharp drop in cases was observed after the implementation of the full lockdown.
source: A sharp drop in cases was observed after the implementation of the full lockdown.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about case trends following the lockdown.

claim: Alpha displaced 20A and 20E (EU1) over time to become the dominant circulating virus lineage by 16 February 2021 (week 6).
source: Alpha then displaced 20 A and 20E (EU1) over time to become the dominant circulating virus lineage by 16 February 2021 (week 6) for the rest of the lockdown period.
evidence: The manuscript states the date when Alpha became dominant.

claim: The first Beta sequence was collected on 22 December 2020.
source: Other VOCs such as Beta (N=422 sequences; first sequence was collected on 22 December 2020) and Gamma (N=350 sequences; first sequence was collected on 27 January 2021) were also detected by random surveillance in The Netherlands around the turn of the year but did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the date of the first Beta sequence collection.

claim: 422 Beta sequences were collected during the study period.
source: Other VOCs such as Beta (N=422 sequences; first sequence was collected on 22 December 2020) and Gamma (N=350 sequences; first sequence was collected on 27 January 2021) were also detected by random surveillance in The Netherlands around the turn of the year but did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of Beta sequences.

claim: The first Gamma sequence was collected on 27 January 2021.
source: Other VOCs such as Beta (N=422 sequences; first sequence was collected on 22 December 2020) and Gamma (N=350 sequences; first sequence was collected on 27 January 2021) were also detected by random surveillance in The Netherlands around the turn of the year but did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the date of the first Gamma sequence collection.

claim: 350 Gamma sequences were collected during the study period.
source: Other VOCs such as Beta (N=422 sequences; first sequence was collected on 22 December 2020) and Gamma (N=350 sequences; first sequence was collected on 27 January 2021) were also detected by random surveillance in The Netherlands around the turn of the year but did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of Gamma sequences.

claim: Beta and Gamma did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
source: Other VOCs such as Beta (N=422 sequences; first sequence was collected on 22 December 2020) and Gamma (N=350 sequences; first sequence was collected on 27 January 2021) were also detected by random surveillance in The Netherlands around the turn of the year but did not circulate to the levels of Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript states this comparison of circulation levels.

claim: Alpha caused a rebound in cases around mid-March 2021.
source: Alpha caused a rebound in cases around mid-March 2021, after which case numbers stabilized and eventually began to decline at the end of April 2021.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about case trends.

claim: Case numbers stabilized and eventually began to decline at the end of April 2021.
source: Alpha caused a rebound in cases around mid-March 2021, after which case numbers stabilized and eventually began to decline at the end of April 2021.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about case trends.

claim: The Dutch government began taking steps to relax restrictions around the end of April 2021, starting with the end of curfew and resumption of higher education during the week of 27 April 2021.
source: The Dutch government began taking steps to relax restrictions around the same time, starting with the end of curfew and resumption of higher education during the week of 27 April 2021.
evidence: The manuscript states the timing and nature of restriction relaxation.

claim: The first Delta sample was collected on 15 April 2021.
source: The first Delta sample was collected in the previous week on 15 April 2021 and continued to accumulate in frequency.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the date of the first Delta sample collection.

claim: By week 25 (29 June 2021), the Delta VOC accounted for 24% of all weekly genomes sequenced.
source: By week 25 (29 June 2021), the Delta VOC accounted for 24% of all weekly genomes sequenced.
evidence: The manuscript states the proportion of Delta sequences at this time point.

claim: Most restrictions were lifted by 26 June 2021.
source: Most restrictions were lifted in the same week by 26 June 2021.
evidence: The manuscript states the date when most restrictions were lifted.

claim: Average nationwide mobility came close to pre-pandemic levels in June 2021 with a mean percentage change relative to pre-pandemic baseline of -5.0% (s.d.=11.0%).
source: As SARS-CoV-2 prevalence declined over time, average nationwide mobility also increased steadily which eventually came close to pre-pandemic levels in June 2021 (mean percentage change relative to pre-pandemic baseline = –5.0% (s.d.=11.0%); Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific mobility data with statistical measures.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 prevalence was at its lowest in June 2021 with only 8,690 reported positive cases that week.
source: SARS-CoV-2 prevalence was at its lowest then with only 8,690 reported positive cases that week.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of cases at this low point.

claim: Within only 1 week after reopening, weekly cases soared above 50,000 on weeks 26 and 27 (6-20 July 2021).
source: Within only 1 week after reopening, however, weekly cases soared above 50,000 on weeks 26 and 27 (6–20 July 2021).
evidence: The manuscript states the rapid increase in cases following reopening.

claim: Over 90% of randomly surveilled genomes were typed as Delta VOCs by mid-July 2021.
source: With most infections attributed to Delta, the novel VOC replaced the Alpha VOC as the dominant lineage within the next 3 weeks as over 90% of randomly surveilled genomes were typed as Delta VOCs by mid-July.
evidence: The manuscript states the proportion of Delta sequences at this time point.

claim: The rapid increase in cases on weeks 26 and 27 was largely attributed to individuals aged between 15 and 30 years.
source: Stratifying the number of weekly reported positive cases by patient age group, the relative proportions in case positive rates remained fairly consistent throughout the study period except for weeks 26 and 27 where the rapid increase in cases was largely attributed to individuals aged between 15 and 30 years (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about age-stratified case data.

claim: One of the reasons behind widespread transmission among young adults in weeks 26 and 27 was super-spreading linked to nightlife venues.
source: One of the reasons behind widespread transmission among young adults then was super-spreading linked to nightlife venues (Koopsen et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Koopsen et al., 2022 to support this claim about super-spreading.

claim: The government shut nightlife establishments down again on 10 July 2021 (week 27).
source: In response, the government shut nightlife establishments down again on 10 July 2021 (week 27).
evidence: The manuscript states the date and nature of this intervention.

claim: Case numbers fell promptly after nightlife establishments were shut down but remained at over 30,000 new cases per week for the rest of the study period.
source: Case numbers fell promptly after but remained at over 30,000 new cases per week for the rest of the study period.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about case trends following the intervention.

claim: Over 99% of randomly surveilled genomes sampled from August 2021 onwards were Delta VOC.
source: The Delta VOC had in principle completely displaced Alpha by then with over 99% of randomly surveilled genomes sampled from August 2021 onwards.
evidence: The manuscript states the proportion of Delta sequences at this time point.

claim: Travel restrictions were imposed on the United Kingdom between December 2020 and March 2021 due to the emergence of Alpha.
source: To deter the introductions of novel VOCs into the Netherlands, travel restrictions were imposed on countries where the VOCs first emerged, including the United Kingdom between December 2020 and March 2021 due to the emergence of Alpha; South Africa and Brazil between January and June 2021 due to Beta and Gamma respectively; and India from April to June 2021 due to Delta.
evidence: The manuscript states the timing and target of these travel restrictions.

claim: Travel restrictions were imposed on South Africa and Brazil between January and June 2021 due to Beta and Gamma respectively.
source: To deter the introductions of novel VOCs into the Netherlands, travel restrictions were imposed on countries where the VOCs first emerged, including the United Kingdom between December 2020 and March 2021 due to the emergence of Alpha; South Africa and Brazil between January and June 2021 due to Beta and Gamma respectively; and India from April to June 2021 due to Delta.
evidence: The manuscript states the timing and targets of these travel restrictions.

claim: Travel restrictions were imposed on India from April to June 2021 due to Delta.
source: To deter the introductions of novel VOCs into the Netherlands, travel restrictions were imposed on countries where the VOCs first emerged, including the United Kingdom between December 2020 and March 2021 due to the emergence of Alpha; South Africa and Brazil between January and June 2021 due to Beta and Gamma respectively; and India from April to June 2021 due to Delta.
evidence: The manuscript states the timing and target of these travel restrictions.

claim: Travel restrictions included a ban on all incoming passenger flights except for those carrying cargo and medical personnel, on top of an entry ban for all non-European Union residents.
source: These travel restrictions include a ban on all incoming passenger flights except for those carrying cargo and medical personnel, on top of an entry ban for all non-European Union residents (Government of the Netherlands, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Government of the Netherlands, 2021 to describe the nature of travel restrictions.

claim: Travel within parts of the Schengen Area in Europe, which includes the Netherlands, remained largely possible during the period of targeted flight restrictions.
source: On the other hand, travel within parts of the Schengen Area in Europe, which includes the Netherlands, remained largely possible during this period.
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about intra-European travel.

claim: All four VOCs were already introduced into the Netherlands prior to the targeted flight restrictions that were imposed on countries where these VOCs first emerged.
source: All four VOCs were already introduced into the Netherlands prior to the targeted flight restrictions that were imposed on countries where these VOCs first emerged.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2.

claim: Multiple likely introduction events from other foreign countries into the Netherlands occurred for all four VOCs (Alpha, n=100; Beta, n=7; Gamma, n=12; Delta, n=213).
source: Importantly, besides countries where travel restrictions were in place, we estimated multiple likely introduction events from other foreign countries into the Netherlands for all four VOCs (Alpha, n=100; Beta, n=7; Gamma, n=12; Delta, n=213).
evidence: The manuscript provides estimated numbers of introduction events based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Many of the estimated regions for ancestral states of VOC introductions were in Europe (Alpha, 71% of all estimated overseas introduction events; Beta, 29%; Gamma, 71%; Delta, 79%).
source: However, many of the estimated regions for these ancestral states were in Europe (Alpha, 71% of all estimated overseas introduction events; Beta, 29%; Gamma, 71%; Delta, 79%; Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages of European introductions based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: European introductions of VOCs continued to occur during the targeted travel ban period.
source: Furthermore, these European introductions continue to occur during the targeted travel ban period.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Many of the nearest overseas neighboring tips to Dutch subtrees were detected in Belgium, Germany, France and Denmark where borders between the Netherlands remained open.
source: Inspecting the nearest phylogenetic ancestral taxon to the aforementioned subtrees, we found that many of these nearest overseas neighboring tips were detected in Belgium, Germany, France and Denmark where borders between the Netherlands remained open as well as other countries (e.g. Spain, U.K., Poland, U.S.) where no targeted travel restrictions were set in place (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: There was no isolated period in time in which VOCs were introduced into the Netherlands - introductions likely occurred repeatedly during the period when these VOCs were also proliferating within the country.
source: There was also no isolated period in time in which these VOCs were introduced into the Netherlands - introductions likely occurred repeatedly during the period when these VOCs were also proliferating within the country.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: For the first four weeks since the initial detection of both Alpha and Delta VOCs, introductions and phylogenetic branch movements were mostly concentrated in the more populous regions of the country, including North and South Holland, Utrecht and North-Brabant.
source: For the first four weeks since the initial detection of both VOCs within the country, introductions and phylogenetic branch movements were mostly concentrated in the more populous regions of the country, including North and South Holland, Utrecht and North-Brabant, forming a core of early dominant locations.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on continuous phylogeographic analyses.

claim: During the initial period after VOC introduction, dispersal events to regions outside of the early dominant source locations occurred but were relatively less frequent.
source: During this period, dispersal events to regions outside of these GGD regions occurred as well but are relatively less frequent.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from phylogeographic analyses.

claim: As local infections were seeded in areas outside early dominant locations, bidirectional exchanges in phylogenetic branches between different regions emerged throughout the country.
source: However, as local infections were seeded in these areas, bidirectional exchanges in phylogenetic branches between different regions emerged throughout the country.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from phylogeographic analyses.

claim: Bidirectional exchanges between regions continued to increase as prevalence of the VOC grew over time, even amidst a strict lockdown in the case of Alpha.
source: These bidirectional exchanges continued to increase as prevalence of the VOC grew over time, even amidst a strict lockdown in the case of Alpha (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from phylogeographic analyses shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the Delta VOC, there was a rapid spike in inter-regional spread upon the week of 22-28 June 2021, with >400% estimated increase in total phylogenetic branch movements by 6 July 2021 (week 26).
source: In particular for the Delta VOC, we observed a rapid spike in inter-regional spread upon the week of 22–28 June 2021, with >400% estimated increase in total phylogenetic branch movements by 6 July 2021 (week 26).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage increase based on phylogeographic analyses.

claim: The significant rise in inter-regional exportation events likely contributed to the soaring case numbers observed between weeks 25 and 27 (22 June - 13 July 2021).
source: This significant rise in inter-regional exportation events likely contributed to the soaring case numbers observed between weeks 25 and 27 (22 June – 13 July 2021).
evidence: The manuscript infers a likely causal relationship between exportation events and case numbers.

claim: The Netherlands is highly vulnerable to importation risks of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants from its regional neighbors due to border policies within the European Union, even if international travel restrictions are in place.
source: Even if international travel restrictions are in place, the Netherlands is still highly vulnerable to importation risks of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants from its regional neighbors due to border policies within the European Union.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: Regional vulnerability to SARS-CoV-2 variant importation is not unique to the Netherlands and has been reported in other European countries as well.
source: As such, this regional vulnerability is not unique to the Netherlands and has been reported in other European countries as well (Lemey et al., 2021; Michaelsen et al., 2021; Osnes et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites three studies to support this claim about regional vulnerability in Europe.

claim: Regional introductions of novel lineages often drive new waves of infections in Europe.
source: Importantly, regional introductions of novel lineages often drive new waves of infections in Europe (Lemey et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lemey et al., 2021 to support this claim.

claim: Prior to September 2020, the dominant variant lineages (20A and 20E (EU1)) that circulated the Netherlands were seeded by imports from its European neighbours.
source: Prior to September 2020, the dominant variant lineages (i.e. 20 A and 20E (EU1)) that circulated the Netherlands were already seeded by imports from its European neighbours (Hodcroft et al., 2021; Nadeau et al., 2021; Oude Munnink et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites three studies to support this claim about earlier variant introductions.

claim: The initial introduction of SARS-CoV-2 in the Netherlands in February 2020 was attributed to travelers who visited Northern Italy where the earliest sustained European SARS-CoV-2 transmission network was seeded.
source: In fact, the initial introduction of SARS-CoV-2 in the Netherlands in February 2020 were attributed to travelers who visited Northern Italy where the earliest sustained European SARS-CoV-2 transmission network was seeded (Oude Munnink et al., 2020; Worobey et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies to support this claim about the initial introduction.

claim: All four VOC lineages detected in the Netherlands up to August 2021 originated mainly from its European neighbors.
source: Here, we showed that all four VOC lineages detected in the country up to August 2021 also originated mainly from its European neighbors.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Regional importation risks of VOCs persisted throughout the period these VOCs circulated the country and overlapped with periods where targeted flight restrictions were imposed on countries where these VOCs first emerged.
source: Importantly, regional importation risks persisted throughout the period these VOCs circulated the country and overlapped with periods where targeted flight restrictions were imposed on countries where these VOCs first emerged.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The Omicron VOC emerged in southern Africa in November 2021.
source: The emergence of the Omicron VOC in southern Africa in November 2021 (Viana et al., 2022) again led to reactionary targeted flight restrictions by several countries in the Global North, including the Netherlands which was still amidst a surging Delta infection wave.
evidence: The manuscript cites Viana et al., 2022 to support this claim about Omicron emergence.

claim: The emergence of Omicron led to reactionary targeted flight restrictions by several countries in the Global North, including the Netherlands.
source: The emergence of the Omicron VOC in southern Africa in November 2021 (Viana et al., 2022) again led to reactionary targeted flight restrictions by several countries in the Global North, including the Netherlands which was still amidst a surging Delta infection wave.
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about policy responses to Omicron.

claim: The Omicron VOC was already detected in the Netherlands in samples collected one week before the imposed flight restriction.
source: However, the Omicron VOC was already detected in samples collected one week before the imposed flight restriction and did not prevent it to rapidly become the dominant VOC circulating in the Netherlands by the end of 2021 (https://www.rivm.nl/coronavirus-covid-19/virus/varianten/omikronvariant).
evidence: The manuscript cites RIVM data to support this claim about Omicron detection timing.

claim: Omicron rapidly became the dominant VOC circulating in the Netherlands by the end of 2021.
source: However, the Omicron VOC was already detected in samples collected one week before the imposed flight restriction and did not prevent it to rapidly become the dominant VOC circulating in the Netherlands by the end of 2021 (https://www.rivm.nl/coronavirus-covid-19/virus/varianten/omikronvariant).
evidence: The manuscript cites RIVM data to support this claim about Omicron dominance.

claim: Travel restrictions are only useful if restrictions barred arrivals from most countries provided that local incidence is low in the first place.
source: Previous studies showed that travel restrictions are only useful if restrictions barred arrivals from most countries provided that local incidence is low in the first place (Russell et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Russell et al., 2021 to support this claim about travel restriction effectiveness.

claim: Early introductions of Alpha and Delta VOCs are more likely found in populous regions of the Netherlands, including Utrecht, North, and South Holland where larger cities are located that are also international and regional travel hubs.
source: We also found that early introductions of VOCs, specifically the Alpha and Delta VOCs, are more likely found in populous regions of the Netherlands, including Utrecht, North, and South Holland where larger cities are located that are also international and regional travel hubs.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogeographic analyses.

claim: The populous regions of Utrecht, North, and South Holland constitute a core cluster of dominant source locations that exported infections to the rest of the country during first few weeks after the VOC's introduction into the Netherlands.
source: These areas constitute a core cluster of dominant source locations that also exported infections to the rest of the country during first few weeks after the VOC's introduction into the Netherlands.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogeographic analyses.

claim: As the number of infections in areas outside of dominant source locations increased over time, bidirectional exchanges became more frequent.
source: As the number of infections in areas outside of these dominant source locations increase over time, bidirectional exchanges would also become more frequent.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from phylogeographic analyses.

claim: Asymmetric spatial spread dynamics enhance the intrinsic transmissibility of Alpha.
source: This type of asymmetric spatial spread dynamics had been previously shown in the U.K. as well and was found to enhance the intrinsic transmissibility of Alpha (Kraemer et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kraemer et al., 2021 to support this claim about spatial spread dynamics.

claim: Enhanced mobility has been linked to the resurgence of outbreaks across Europe.
source: Additionally, enhanced mobility has also been previously linked to the resurgence of outbreaks across Europe (Hodcroft et al., 2021; Lemey et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies to support this claim about mobility and outbreaks.

claim: Increased mobility and population mixing drove the rapid dissemination of Delta in the U.K.
source: Recent work also showed that increased mobility and population mixing drove the rapid dissemination of Delta in the U.K. (McCrone et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites McCrone et al., 2021 to support this claim about Delta dissemination.

claim: The asymmetric exportation frequencies from dominant source locations, increased human mobility in weeks 25-27 across the country, and the intrinsic higher transmissibility of Delta relative to Alpha likely all contributed to the widespread spike in cases in the Netherlands.
source: While our analyses do not provide a causal relationship between the relaxation of non-pharmaceutical interventions and frequency of export events, the asymmetric exportation frequencies from dominant source locations, increased human mobility in weeks 25–27 across the country as well as the intrinsic higher transmissibility of Delta relative to Alpha likely all contributed to the widespread spike in cases in the Netherlands.
evidence: The manuscript infers this likely contribution based on multiple factors.

claim: Novel and fitter variants of SARS-CoV-2 will likely continue to emerge in the future.
source: Novel and fitter variants of SARS-CoV-2 will likely continue to emerge in the future.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about future variant emergence.

claim: Unless well-coordinated actions are taken across Europe to mitigate importation risks, targeted travel restrictions implemented by individual European countries will neither prevent nor slow down the introduction of novel variants.
source: Our results, along with others, show that unless well-coordinated actions are taken across Europe to mitigate importation risks (Ruktanonchai et al., 2020), targeted travel restrictions implemented by individual European countries will neither prevent nor slow down the introduction of novel variants.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the study findings and cites Ruktanonchai et al., 2020.

claim: Both the Alpha and Delta VOCs were first detected in the early dominant source locations, usually those that are more populous with greater international connections, and circulated mostly within these areas during the initial period after introduction.
source: Both the Alpha and Delta VOCs were first detected in the early dominant source locations, usually those that are more populous with greater international connections, and circulated mostly within these areas during the initial period after introduction.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on phylogeographic analyses.

claim: A robust level of surveillance efforts should be maintained in dominant source locations to provide timely actionable information on novel variant detection as well as infection control.
source: As such, a robust level of surveillance efforts should still be maintained in these dominant source locations to provide timely actionable information on novel variant detection as well as infection control.
evidence: The manuscript recommends this surveillance strategy based on study findings.

claim: A minimal level of clinical diagnostic testing capacity should be maintained to ensure clinical genomic surveillance remains sensitive enough for early detection of novel variants.
source: These surveillance efforts should encompass a minimal level of clinical diagnostic testing capacity be maintained to ensure clinical genomic surveillance remains sensitive enough for early detection of novel variants (Han et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Han et al., 2022 to support this recommendation.

claim: Wastewater surveillance could be included to facilitate early variant detection and identify cryptic transmissions amid falling testing rates.
source: Wastewater surveillance could also be included to facilitate early variant detection and identify cryptic transmissions amid falling testing rates (Karthikeyan et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Karthikeyan et al., 2022 to support this recommendation.

claim: The Alpha VOC was first reported in the United Kingdom during the fall of 2020.
source: The Alpha VOC was first reported in the United Kingdom (U.K.) during the fall of 2020 and found to be 43–90% more transmissible (Davies et al., 2021a; Volz et al., 2021) with greater mortality risks (Davies et al., 2021b; Grint et al., 2021) than previously existing variants.
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about Alpha emergence.

claim: The Alpha VOC was found to be 43-90% more transmissible than previously existing variants.
source: The Alpha VOC was first reported in the United Kingdom (U.K.) during the fall of 2020 and found to be 43–90% more transmissible (Davies et al., 2021a; Volz et al., 2021) with greater mortality risks (Davies et al., 2021b; Grint et al., 2021) than previously existing variants.
evidence: The manuscript cites Davies et al., 2021a and Volz et al., 2021 to support this claim about Alpha transmissibility.

claim: The Alpha VOC has greater mortality risks than previously existing variants.
source: The Alpha VOC was first reported in the United Kingdom (U.K.) during the fall of 2020 and found to be 43–90% more transmissible (Davies et al., 2021a; Volz et al., 2021) with greater mortality risks (Davies et al., 2021b; Grint et al., 2021) than previously existing variants.
evidence: The manuscript cites Davies et al., 2021b and Grint et al., 2021 to support this claim about Alpha mortality.

claim: Alpha has 17 amino acid mutations.
source: Of the 17 amino acids mutations found in Alpha, N501Y in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike protein was predicted to increase binding to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors (Starr et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of mutations in Alpha.

claim: N501Y mutation in the receptor-binding domain of the spike protein in Alpha was predicted to increase binding to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors.
source: Of the 17 amino acids mutations found in Alpha, N501Y in the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike protein was predicted to increase binding to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors (Starr et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Starr et al., 2020 to support this claim about N501Y mutation.

claim: N501Y is a common mutation found in Beta and Gamma.
source: This is also a common mutation found in Beta (Tegally et al., 2021) and Gamma (Faria et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Tegally et al., 2021 and Faria et al., 2021 to support this claim about N501Y in Beta and Gamma.

claim: The Delta VOC was first identified in India in October 2020.
source: On the other hand, the Delta VOC, first identified in India in October 2020 (Cherian et al., 2021), encodes P681R mutation in the furin cleavage site in spike protein and R203M mutation in the nucleocapsid protein that improves infectivity (Syed et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Cherian et al., 2021 to support this claim about Delta emergence.

claim: Delta encodes P681R mutation in the furin cleavage site in spike protein and R203M mutation in the nucleocapsid protein that improves infectivity.
source: On the other hand, the Delta VOC, first identified in India in October 2020 (Cherian et al., 2021), encodes P681R mutation in the furin cleavage site in spike protein and R203M mutation in the nucleocapsid protein that improves infectivity (Syed et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Syed et al., 2021 to support this claim about Delta mutations.

claim: Delta has been linked to increased disease severity, as well as greater and longer viral shedding.
source: Delta has also been linked to increased disease severity, as well as greater and longer viral shedding (Ong et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ong et al., 2021 to support this claim about Delta disease characteristics.

claim: Delta was first detected in the U.K. in April 2021.
source: In the U.K., where the VOC was first detected in April 2021, epidemiological modelling estimated the VOC to be 40–80% more transmissible than Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about Delta detection in the U.K.

claim: Epidemiological modelling estimated Delta to be 40-80% more transmissible than Alpha in the U.K.
source: In the U.K., where the VOC was first detected in April 2021, epidemiological modelling estimated the VOC to be 40–80% more transmissible than Alpha.
evidence: The manuscript states this estimate from epidemiological modeling.

claim: The four VOCs (Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta) were introduced into the Netherlands, with Alpha and Delta subsequently dominating infections in the country in 2021.
